core: Animation as a filmmaking medium that builds the illusion of movement from a rapid succession of still images
The principle of the constructed frame: in animation every frame is made, not recorded, which animators control completely
Key techniques: drawn/cel animation, stop-motion, computer-generated animation, and rotoscoping, including the 2D versus 3D distinction
Why animation is a medium rather than a genre, and why it is not a children's format by definition
How animation uses the film language of editing, sound, and cinematography in frame-by-frame production

claims.claim: Animation is the art of making inanimate objects appear to move: it creates the appearance of movement from a rapid succession of still images, each of which is constructed rather than recorded as live action.

The theory of the animated image preceded cinema by about half a century: pre-cinema devices such as the phenakistoscope (1832), the zoetrope (1834), and Émile Reynaud's 1876 adaptation for theatrical projection showed that drawings of the stages of an action, presented in fast succession, are perceived as continuous movement.

Early animation used several frame-by-frame techniques: hand-drawn animation, stop-motion (photograph an object, reposition it, photograph again), and clay, puppet, and cut-out animation, as seen in works such as J. Stuart Blackton's Humorous Phases of Funny Faces (1906), Émile Cohl's Fantasmagorie (1908), and Winsor McCay's Gertie the Dinosaur (1914).
Rotoscoping traces live-action footage frame by frame to guide drawn animation; the Fleischer brothers developed the process and exploited it in their Out of the Inkwell series (1919-29).

Synchronized sound entered animation with cartoons such as Steamboat Willie (1928), and animation handles the film language of editing, sound, and cinematography through planned, frame-by-frame construction rather than through capturing live performances.

Computer-generated animation produces images with software; Toy Story (1995) is described as the first entirely computer-animated feature-length film, and 3D computer animation models objects, lights, and virtual cameras in a virtual space rendered frame by frame.

Animation is a medium and a set of techniques, not a genre: genres such as comedy, drama, and adventure cut across it, and although much animated content is aimed at children, the medium has carried adult-oriented and serious material for over a century, including McCay's 1918 re-creation of the sinking of the Lusitania and early work tied to adult newspaper comics.

Because no live action is recorded, an animated work's motion, timing, and cuts are planned in advance (for example, through storyboarding and timing sheets), so the 'illusion of life' results from controlled construction rather than from accidental capture.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Claims about 'firsts' in animation history (first film-based animation, first animated feature) are contested and depend on definitions.
positions: Encyclopaedia Britannica hedges that 'firsts of any kind are never easy to establish' and identifies J. Stuart Blackton's Humorous Phases of Funny Faces (1906) as the first film-based animation 'appears to be'.

Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was not the first animated feature, but the first to use up-to-the-minute techniques and to receive a wide, Hollywood-style release.
Encyclopaedia Britannica describes Toy Story (1995) as the first entirely computer-animated feature-length film, while earlier features and shorts had incorporated computer techniques.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids absolute 'first ever' claims, uses Britannica's hedged phrasing, and attributes each dated event to its source.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'Persistence of vision' is the traditional explanation for why rapid still images read as movement, but vision research treats the phenomenon as more complex than a simple retinal afterimage.
positions: Encyclopaedia Britannica describes early experimenters as discovering 'the principle of persistence of vision.'
Open Oregon's OER chapter relates early animation to 'persistence of vision' devices such as the zoetrope while focusing on how rapid successive images create the look of motion.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson phrases the phenomenon as viewers perceiving rapid successive images as continuous movement, which both sources support, and does not assert a settled physiological mechanism.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated phase-3 draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Animation is a foundational concept in Film & Media Studies') with no source-grounded factual claims about the medium, its techniques, or its history.
The draft's definition of animation as a 'toolbox label' and its sample questions treated the topic as a vocabulary lesson rather than a filmmaking medium.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with a source-grounded lesson defining animation as a constructed medium built from successive frames.

Added verified historical anchors (phenakistoscope 1832, zoetrope 1834, Reynaud 1876; Blackton 1906, Cohl 1908, McCay 1914; Fleischer rotoscope; Steamboat Willie 1928; Snow White 1937; Toy Story 1995) while hedging contested 'first' claims.
Framed animation as a medium rather than a genre and as a medium without an inherent age group, with the range claim kept general and source-supported.
Added five source-linked questions with verified four-option keys distributed across positions A, B, C, and D.
Excluded genre, representation, and documentary content as owned by sibling topics.
rightsIssues: Encyclopaedia Britannica is proprietary; it was used as REFERENCE_ONLY for verifiable facts, and no Britannica prose was reproduced.
Library of Congress and Open Oregon sources are openly licensed (LoC government content; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for Open Oregon); the lesson synthesizes facts into original prose.
No film dialogue, clips, screenshots, stills, or descriptions of copyrighted scenes were reproduced; all examples are original invented scenarios.

The lesson uses original synthesis only.
